teaching.prerequisite_note: Use quoted arguments, printf, test, if, redirection and exit status from earlier scripting units. This lesson introduces extended regular expressions (ERE), not a new shell language.

concepts.title: A shape rule instead of exact text
concepts.text: A regular expression describes text to select. grep -F looks for literal text; grep -E reads a pattern. Put the pattern in single quotes so the shell passes it unchanged. Shell case patterns and ERE are different: [0-9]* in ERE means zero or more digits, not a digit followed by arbitrary text.

concepts.title: Choose a complete record
concepts.text: A normal grep search can find a fragment anywhere. ^ marks the start of one line and $ its end. ^OPEN: matches a beginning; ^OPEN:ab$ matches only that complete line. grep reads lines, not a multi-line record.

concepts.title: Choose characters and amounts
concepts.text: [a-z] means one ASCII lowercase letter; [0-9] means one ASCII digit; [[:digit:]] is a named ASCII digit class here. [[:alnum:]] includes ASCII digits and letters in both cases. {2} means exactly two of the item before it; {1,3} means one through three. + means one or more, * zero or more, and ? zero or one. A dot . means any one byte, not a literal dot; write \. for a literal dot.

concepts.title: Group a choice
concepts.text: (OPEN|HOLD) means either whole word. Parentheses group the choice; | separates alternatives. Keep shared anchors outside a group when the whole choice must fit one line: ^(OPEN|HOLD):[a-z]{2}$.

concepts.title: Keep evidence and interpret status
concepts.text: -n prefixes selected lines with their original line number and a colon; skipped lines still count. grep returns 0 if it selected anything, 1 for no selected lines, and 2 for a recognized pattern/read error. A selected final line gets a newline even if the source had none. -- ends options; the following quoted pattern and filename remain separate arguments. A literal - is still the stdin marker after --, so this named-file assignment rejects it.

concepts.text: grep -q is quiet: it prints no selected text, but its status still answers the question. if runs the next command and takes its first branch for status 0. Pipe one preserved line from printf into grep -Eq; printf uses a fixed %s format, not the row as code or a format.

concepts.title: Reject the opposite when useful
concepts.text: -v reverses selection. With -q it quietly reports whether a nonmatching line exists. This is useful for preflight checks. Do not confuse grep status 1 (no selected line) with a broken program; decide what no match means for your task.

concepts.title: A range is not a collection of words
concepts.text: [a-z] chooses one character. (lab|store) chooses one of two words; [lab|store] would choose only one character from the bracket contents. Keep parentheses around a complete word choice and anchors around the complete record.

concepts.title: Keep going without hiding mistakes
concepts.text: Count physical input lines even when a row is invalid. Print each reason to stderr, keep checking later rows, and report separate valid/invalid totals. Finish with status 1 if any row needed attention; one later good row must not erase that fact.

concepts.title: Keep a final line even without a newline
concepts.text: IFS= read -r line preserves spaces and backslashes. read may store a final line but report end-of-input; || test -n "$line" lets the loop process that retained text. A blank line still arrives successfully and must be assessed, not silently skipped.

teaching.example:
for tag in 'A-12' 'A-7' 'b-34'; do
  if printf '%s\n' "$tag" | grep -Eq -- '^[A-Z]-[0-9]{2}$'; then
    printf 'Ready: %s\n' "$tag"
  else
    printf 'Review: %s\n' "$tag" >&2
  fi
done

teaching.try_change: Change A-7 to A-07 and Run: it now meets the two-digit format and moves to stdout. Restore A-7 to reproduce the original example.

scenario.retry_guidance: Compare the selected case’s expected and actual output, status and files. Check anchors before broadening a pattern; an empty successful report differs from a no-match filter. Retry without changing the supplied inputs.

if test "$#" -ne 3; then
  printf 'Usage: incident-report FIRST SECOND REPORT\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
simple_name() {
  case "$1" in ''|*[!a-z0-9.-]*) return 1 ;; esac
  printf '%s\n' "$1" | grep -Eq -- "$2"
}
for input in "$1" "$2"; do
  if simple_name "$input" '^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,11}\.log$'; then true
  else printf 'Choose simple .log input names.\n' >&2; exit 2
  fi

else printf 'Choose a simple .report destination.\n' >&2; exit 2
fi

  printf 'Choose two distinct input files.\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
for input in "$1" "$2"; do
  if test -f "$input"; then true
  else printf 'Missing input: %s\n' "$input" >&2; exit 2
  fi
  if grep -Evq -- '^$|^(INFO|FAIL|DENY):[[:lower:]][[:alnum:]-]{0,7}:[0-9]{3}$' "$input"; then
    printf 'Malformed input: %s\n' "$input" >&2
    exit 2
  fi
done

  printf 'Source: %s\n' "$input" >> "$3"

concepts.title: Validation comes before selection
concepts.text: A broad incident filter can hide malformed records as if they never existed. First verify that every nonblank record has the agreed shape, including INFO records; only then select FAIL and DENY. The example uses parcel records instead of logs.

concepts.title: Quiet inverted selection finds a bad row
concepts.text: grep -Evq returns 0 when at least one row does not fit the whole format. That means refuse publication. A completely empty file has no bad rows; empty separator lines are allowed only because this task says so. Group alternatives with their own ^ and $ when admitting an empty line.

concepts.title: Names also need an explicit policy
concepts.text: The assignment chooses simple basenames with different .log and .report suffixes. A literal dot needs \. in an ERE. grep checks lines, so reject any newline in a filename before using it to validate a single name. The earlier shell case pattern *[!a-z0-9.-]* finds any character outside lowercase letters, digits, dot and hyphen, including a newline; put hyphen last so it stays literal. This is a character guard, not the complete filename shape. Reject unsafe names before test, reads or >. The suffix rule prevents report/input collisions; it is a task-specific policy, not a universal filesystem security check.

concepts.title: An ordinary no-match is still useful evidence
concepts.text: One valid log can contain no incidents. Its section heading must still appear. A grep returning 1 must not erase the other source’s incidents or make the whole validated report fail. Exit 0 explicitly after successful publication.

concepts.title: Know what this protects
concepts.text: > replaces an existing destination as soon as that redirection runs. Complete all predictable input checks first. This exercise protects against its listed preflight failures; it does not model atomic rename, disk failure, locks, simultaneous writers or real-time log changes.
